text:
You've probably never heard of Beignet Investor. It's named after a fried pastry from New Orleans. But in October twenty twenty-five, it borrowed twenty-seven point three billion dollars, from the kind of funds that manage pensions and insurance money. All of it to pay for one building: Meta's Hyperion AI data center, in rural Louisiana.
Within days, its bonds were trading at a hundred and ten cents on the dollar. Everyone wanted in.
Then the biggest lender quietly sold about three billion dollars of them, while the price was still high.
In September, the bonds hit a record low, on a day Meta's stock was soaring. By October, they were down to around ninety-two cents.

So who lent the money? What did Meta promise them? And why is the bond market nervous about a company the stock market loves?
We're going to follow this one bond, from the day it was born to the price it trades at now. Every number on screen comes from a filing, a ratings agency, or a named report. The sources are in the description.
One thing up front. Nothing here is illegal. The structure is disclosed, and no one is accused of wrongdoing. That's exactly why it matters. Because this is how the AI boom is being paid for.

Richland Parish, Louisiana. Farmland in the north-east corner of the state. This is where Meta is building Hyperion.
Mark Zuckerberg has said it will cover a significant part of the footprint of Manhattan. To power it, the local utility, Entergy, is building gas plants. Three were approved in twenty twenty-five. In March twenty twenty-six, Meta agreed to fund seven more. Ten plants, more than seven gigawatts, according to Entergy. Fortune estimated the ten plants alone would cost nearly eleven billion dollars. And Meta is also paying for two hundred forty miles of new transmission lines.
Getting there was its own fight. In August twenty twenty-five, Louisiana's Public Service Commission approved the first three plants, four votes to one. In April twenty twenty-six, it voted, again four to one, to fast-track the request for seven more. Critics, like the Union of Concerned Scientists, argue that local electricity customers could be left with part of the bill. And in August twenty twenty-six, the commission voted to overturn a judge's ruling that would have forced Meta to disclose details like its projected energy use and jobs.
The data center itself: about twenty-seven billion dollars in development costs.
And Hyperion is only one project. For twenty twenty-six, Meta expects to spend between one hundred thirty-five and one hundred forty-five billion dollars on capital expenditures. In the third quarter alone, it spent almost thirty-five billion.
Meta can afford a lot. That same quarter, revenue was sixty-four point six billion dollars, up twenty-six percent.
But every giant company runs into the same problem. Borrow twenty-seven billion dollars for one building, and that's twenty-seven billion dollars of new debt on your balance sheet. Ratings agencies see it. Bond investors see it. It changes what everyone charges you to borrow.
So Meta did something else. Instead of Meta borrowing the money, someone else would. Someone Meta only partly owns.

On October twenty-first, twenty twenty-five, Meta announced a joint venture with funds managed by Blue Owl Capital, a private investment firm.
The split: Blue Owl's funds own eighty percent. Meta keeps twenty.
Blue Owl put in about seven billion dollars in cash. And Meta, on day one, received a one-time payment from the venture of about three billion dollars. Meta was paid to bring the project in.
The rest of the money came from a bond. A company set up for the deal, Beignet Investor L L C, sold twenty-seven point three billion dollars of notes. The interest rate: six point five eight one percent a year. The final maturity: May twenty forty-nine. Almost twenty-four years away.
S and P rated it A plus. That's one notch below Meta's own rating of double A minus.
So why would lenders treat a company that's only twenty percent Meta almost like Meta itself? Because of two promises.
Promise one: the lease. Meta rents the finished buildings from the venture, and that rent is what pays the lenders. But the lease runs in four-year initial terms, with options to extend. At the end of a term, Meta can leave.
Promise two: the guarantee. If Meta leaves during the first sixteen years of operations, and certain conditions are met, Meta makes a capped cash payment to the venture. It's called a residual value guarantee. It's the reason this bond looks almost like Meta's own debt.
And here's the clever part. Meta's filings describe the venture as an entity it does not consolidate. In plain English: the debt is real. It just isn't on Meta's balance sheet.

So who bought it? Mostly one firm. Pimco, one of the world's biggest bond managers, anchored the deal with about eighteen billion dollars, according to Bloomberg. Bond managers like Pimco invest money for pension funds, insurers, and ordinary savers.
The rest went to other big investors, through a private offering sold only to large institutions.
And the demand was enormous. Within days, the bonds traded as high as one hundred and ten cents on the dollar.
Here's what that means, because the whole story runs on it. A bond starts at one hundred, its face value. If investors want it badly, they pay more than a hundred. If they get nervous, they pay less. And when the price falls, the yield, the return a new buyer locks in, goes up.
So a hundred and ten meant one thing. Lenders were fighting to get in.
Nine days after the venture was announced, Meta sold thirty billion dollars of its own bonds. Orders hit about a hundred and twenty-five billion dollars, a record for a U.S. corporate bond sale, according to Bloomberg. The longest of those bonds runs forty years.
Everyone believed. The demand for AI was real. Meta's revenue was growing. And six and a half percent was a high rate for something rated A plus.
Almost everyone. One buyer was already doing something else.

In October twenty twenty-six, Bloomberg reported what Pimco had done. Within six to eight months of the deal, Pimco sold about three billion dollars of Beignet bonds, while they were still trading above a hundred. According to Bloomberg, it now holds about half as much of its Meta position, and of a similar deal it anchored for Oracle.
That Oracle deal is a warning of its own. A data center campus in Saline Township, Michigan, built for Oracle. Fourteen billion dollars of bonds, sold in April twenty twenty-six. Pimco bought about ten billion of them. According to Bloomberg, citing trade data, those bonds were issued at ninety-eight point seven cents, and have dropped to around eighty-eight.
Pimco hasn't explained its trades. A representative declined to comment. Selling part of a position isn't wrongdoing, and it isn't proof of anything. Big funds rebalance all the time. And Pimco is still among the largest holders of both deals.
Bloomberg also reported that Pimco passed on some of the AI debt deals that came after, including SoftBank's roughly eleven billion dollar junk bond.
But look at the timing. The firm that anchored the deal cut its stake while other buyers were still paying more than face value.
And then the price started to fall.

By late July twenty twenty-six, the Beignet bonds were around ninety-six cents.
On September twenty-third, they hit a record low of ninety-four point four, on a day Meta's stock was soaring. The stock market and the bond market were looking at the same company, and seeing different things.
By mid-October, the bonds had slipped to just under ninety-two.
That's not a default. Meta is paying. But on paper, anyone who bought at a hundred is down about eight cents on every dollar.
Then came the sequel. In July twenty twenty-six, Meta did it again. A new venture, for a data center in El Paso, Texas, with BlackRock-managed entities owning eighty percent. The bond was issued by a company called Sopaipilla Investor. Another pastry. About twelve and a half billion dollars, due in twenty forty-eight.
Now look at the price. It yielded about seven and a half percent, more than the Louisiana bond. And orders were about twenty billion dollars, roughly one point six times the deal.
Compare that with the hundred and twenty-five billion dollars of orders Meta's own bonds drew nine months earlier. Same company. Same idea. Investors still showed up. But they wanted more interest, and far fewer of them were fighting to get in.

So what is Meta actually on the hook for? It's in the filings.
Meta reports something called its maximum exposure to loss: the most it could lose on these data center ventures if everything went wrong. At the end of twenty twenty-five, that number was about forty-six billion dollars. By September thirtieth, twenty twenty-six, with a second venture in Texas included, it was sixty-eight point four billion.
Inside that, the residual value guarantees, the promise to pay if Meta leaves, rose from about twenty-eight billion dollars to forty-one and a half billion.
Remember, Meta owns twenty percent of these ventures. Its possible loss is far bigger than twenty percent.
And the ratings agencies noticed. On October thirtieth, twenty twenty-six, S and P cut its outlook on Meta from stable to negative. It kept the double A minus rating. But it said Meta's future lease obligations had reached three hundred fifty-five point seven billion dollars, against about eighty-one billion dollars of long-term debt. S and P counts leases like these as debt.
Its math is simple. When the new leases start, S and P expects Meta's adjusted leverage to climb from about zero point one times in twenty twenty-five, to one point three times in twenty twenty-eight. Above one times, on a lasting basis, is where S and P said a downgrade could come.
It expects Meta's free operating cash flow to show a deficit of thirty-nine billion dollars in twenty twenty-six, and seventy-one billion in twenty twenty-seven. And it expects Meta to cover its twenty twenty-eight shortfall entirely with debt.
S and P also said Meta's ability to make money from its AI investments is more limited than its peers'. Meta's answer: we respectfully disagree.
So off the balance sheet never meant off the hook. The guarantees were in the footnotes the whole time. Now the people who rate Meta's debt are adding them back.

Now, the real number. And it isn't a price. It's a date.
The Beignet bond runs until twenty forty-nine.
Meta's lease runs in four-year terms.
The guarantee covers sixteen years of operations.
And the computers inside the building? Meta's own annual report says it depreciates most of its servers and network equipment over five and a half years. That was already an extension. Before twenty twenty-five, it used four to five. Meta said that one change would cut its twenty twenty-five depreciation by about two point nine billion dollars. Even so, depreciation on servers and network gear reached thirteen point three six billion dollars that year, up from seven point three two billion two years earlier. The machines are getting more expensive, and they don't last.
So picture the timeline. Lenders get paid back over almost twenty-four years. The machines that make the building valuable wear out, on Meta's own accounting, in five and a half. The tenant can leave every four. And the guarantee is shorter than the bond.
That's the mismatch. A long loan against something that ages fast.
And it isn't just Meta. The Kansas City Fed found that AI firms went from two percent of all investment-grade bond issuance in twenty twenty-three, to ten percent in twenty twenty-six. Their bonds run longer than the market's average of about ten years. And much of this lending sits outside the banking system. Its conclusion: the build-out will have lasting consequences for the people who lend to it.
Here's the fair version. The demand for AI is real. Meta's revenue is growing fast. In November twenty twenty-six, it raised fifteen billion dollars more, and orders reached as much as fifty-eight billion. Days later, Meta sold nine billion euros of bonds in Europe, its first ever, and the longest of them won't be repaid until twenty sixty-five. Lenders still want Meta's debt.
But the price has changed. A year ago, Meta's thirty-year bonds paid five point six two five percent. Its newest thirty-year notes pay seven and a half. The boom was cheap to fund. Now it isn't.

So who is holding the bond behind Meta's biggest AI data center? Pimco, with a smaller stake than it started with. Other big funds. And through them, the pensions, insurers and savers whose money they manage.
If you want to follow it from here, watch three things. The Beignet bond price. The maximum exposure to loss Meta reports every quarter. And Louisiana, where regulators are due to vote on the seven new gas plants for Hyperion.
None of this means the boom collapses. It means the risk moved, from Meta's balance sheet to the people who lent the money. This isn't investment advice. It's how the deal works.
Tell me in the comments: which AI deal should we follow next?
And if you want to see what happens when the money machine inside a company grows bigger than the company itself, watch this next. How a bank inside General Electric nearly broke it.
